## Abstract

Gait dynamics are usually summarised by asymptotic stability (Floquet multipliers), and data-driven dynamical models (neural ODEs, reservoir computers, sparse regression, spectral-submanifold reductions) are increasingly fitted to walking. But walking never reaches the asymptotic regime: it is perturbed every stride and corrected by noisy feedback, so what governs it is the transient response over the next few strides, which eigenvalues of non-normal return maps miss and which short, noisy records estimate poorly. Studying transients asks specific things of a model. Above all it must predict: run on its own from the current state, it should forecast held-out strides, on the cycle and after perturbations, with skill beyond reference forecasts that need no dynamics (the mean cycle, the last stride). It should also keep the right cycle over long rollouts, give one answer per data set, behave predictably under measurement noise, and work from modest data. Against these requirements, on realistic oscillators, SLIP and human gait, dynamical models forecast far beyond the reference where the data hold predictable dynamics, and barely beyond it on noise-driven data. Expressive models are sometimes the best forecasters but often blow up, settle on the wrong attractor or depend on the seed. Hankel-DMD, linear in delay coordinates, forecasts consistently (close to the best model in most cases and never far below the reference), keeps the right cycle in 92% of cases, gives one convex answer, has an analysable and correctable bias and fits in seconds, with known limits (a neutral cycle amplitude, a need for transients). No model recovers transverse dynamics that passive on-cycle data do not contain, and 15-s gait trials do not identify stride-to-stride dynamics, so we recommend perturbation experiments and reporting finite-time response with its uncertainty.

## Introduction

<!-- OUTLINE §1 ¶1 --> Walking is regulated stride by stride, and understanding how the nervous system and the body jointly produce, and correct, each stride is central to explaining gait impairment and designing interventions.

<!-- OUTLINE §1 ¶2 --> The oldest route to gait dynamics is mechanistic: low-dimensional templates and detailed musculoskeletal simulations that generate walking from physical principles. These reproduce typical gait but are hard to fit to an individual, and they often fail to predict changes in kinematics [@winner2023].

<!-- OUTLINE §1 ¶3 --> A second tradition summarises gait dynamics with stability and variability statistics computed directly from kinematics, not with a generative model [@dingwell2000; @dingwell2006; @bruijn2013].

<!-- OUTLINE §1 ¶4 --> A third, newer tradition fits dynamical models to gait data. The methods range from linear step-to-step maps to deep sequence models, and each trades interpretability for expressiveness differently [@revzen2012; @winner2023].

<!-- OUTLINE §1 ¶5 --> The stability tradition and most model-based work aim at the same quantity, asymptotic stability, in a system that never reaches the asymptotic regime. And there is little systematic evidence on whether expressive data-driven models predict walking beyond its average cycle, or recover the dynamics around it.

<!-- OUTLINE §1 ¶6 --> We argue that for a gait perturbed and noisily corrected every stride, the right target is the transient, finite-time response, not asymptotic stability. We derive what a data-driven model must do to study that response, above all predict it, and why gait data make it hard. We test expressive and linear models against these requirements and find that linear models in Hankel (delay) coordinates meet them best. Finally, we show what linear models reveal on real gait, and where 15-s trials stop every model.

## Asymptotic stability is the wrong target for gait

<!-- OUTLINE §2 ¶1 --> Floquet multipliers answer a precise question: how fast, asymptotically, a perturbation shrinks per cycle. That made them the natural stability measure for gait [@dingwell2006].

<!-- OUTLINE §2 ¶2 --> Gait is perturbed every stride by intrinsic noise and by the environment, so what governs behaviour is the response over the next one to three strides, the transient. Asymptotic multipliers can miss it entirely.

<!-- OUTLINE §2 ¶3 --> When every stride is kicked and every stride is corrected, the deviation at any stride is the sum of the decaying responses to all earlier kicks. Stride-to-stride variability is the transient response, sampled continuously, and how deviations are corrected reveals the control strategy.

<!-- OUTLINE §2 ¶4 --> Even for a textbook Van der Pol oscillator, the monodromy matrix and the stride-to-stride return map are non-normal: their eigenvectors are far from orthogonal, and within-cycle variational dynamics amplify perturbations transiently before they decay (@fig-nonnormal) [@trefethen2005; @hess2026nonnormality].

![**Eigenvalues are not the whole story: oscillators amplify perturbations before they decay.** Ground truth from forward-integrated variational equations, no fitting: coupled FitzHugh–Nagumo (FHN), Van der Pol (nonlinearity 0.1–2.0), Stuart–Landau, and SLIP walking open loop and with speed feedback. Norms are in observed coordinates (each variable scaled by its SD along the cycle), worst case over the phase at which the perturbation arrives. (A) Distance from the cycle after a perturbation, relative to its size, against time since the perturbation; dashed, the multiplier's prediction. (B) Peak within-cycle transverse amplification against the transverse multiplier; shaded, multipliers reported for human walking (≈0.3–0.8). (C) Stride to stride: worst-case growth of the n-stride transverse map against the eigenvalue prediction ρⁿ (dashed). (D) Deviation from the unperturbed trajectory after n cycles, including lasting phase shifts; the multiplier along the cycle is 1, so the eigenvalue prediction is 1.](figures/Fig4_nonnormality){#fig-nonnormal fig-alt="Four panels: perturbation size against time for several oscillators, peak amplification against multiplier, n-stride growth against the eigenvalue prediction, and lasting deviation after n cycles."}

<!-- OUTLINE §2 ¶6 --> We propose characterising gait by its finite-time response operators: how deviations at one stride propagate, amplify and redistribute across joints over the next few strides. These are quantities that linear models expose directly, and a model that predicts the next few strides from the current state, including after a perturbation, is a model of exactly this response.

## What a model of gait transients must do

<!-- OUTLINE §3 ¶1 --> A model is useful for gait to the extent that it predicts: from the current state, what the next strides will do, including after a perturbation. Studying transients adds requirements that short-horizon prediction alone does not guarantee:

1. **Predictive skill in autonomous rollouts (R1).** Run from the current state with no data fed back, the model forecasts held-out data over the next few strides, on the cycle and after perturbations.
2. **Faithful long-run behaviour (R2).** Over long rollouts it keeps the right cycle (no blow-up, wrong period or collapse) and returns to it after a perturbation, evidence that it has learned the vector field around the cycle.
3. **One answer (R3).** The same data give the same model and the same stability readout across seeds and nearby hyperparameters, so that differences between people are not fitting noise.
4. **Predictable behaviour under measurement noise (R4).** Its estimates are insensitive to kinematic noise, or biased in a way that can be analysed and corrected.
5. **Modest data needs (R5).** It works from tens of strides and a few channels, and shows when the data cannot support an answer.
6. **Cheap and inspectable (R6).** It fits fast enough for cross-validation and bootstrap, with spectra and modes that can be checked.

We measure prediction as weather forecasts are measured, against reference forecasts that need no dynamics: the mean cycle at the current phase and the last stride repeated, which play the roles of climatology and persistence. The references are not candidate models, since they have no state and cannot be started off the cycle; they define zero skill (skill = 1 − model error / reference error). Because the mean cycle holds all but a few percent of a trial's variance (Figure [-@fig-gait-mean]B), skill is reported on the deviations from it as well as on the full signal. Errors are validation errors, computed on held-out data and by autonomous rollout rather than one-step (teacher-forced) prediction. Across every setting of the benchmark's DMD and ESN tuning grids, rollout validation errors rank settings by their test forecast error (median rank correlation 0.71–0.88), and one-step errors do not (−0.19 to 0.40). Choosing ESN settings by in-sample one-step error picks models that blow up, while choosing by several held-out rollouts from different starts keeps the right cycle as often as choosing on the test data itself (@suppfig-validation).

<!-- TODO R1: the benchmark's tuning still chooses by one held-out rollout; decide whether to switch it to the
multistart rollout (OUTLINE to-do 7). Neural-ODE one-step validation needs refits with saved weights. -->

<!-- OUTLINE §3 ¶2 --> Neural ODEs, SINDy, reservoir computers and DMD have their clearest successes on systems with fixed governing equations, high signal-to-noise ratio, abundant snapshots, and dynamics observed through their transients [@chen2018; @brunton2016; @pathak2018].

<!-- OUTLINE §3 ¶3 --> In walking, mechanics and neural control form one feedback loop. Passive recordings of the loop cannot separate plant from controller, a classic result in closed-loop system identification.

<!-- OUTLINE §3 ¶4 --> Because the controller suppresses deviations, walking data stay close to the limit cycle. The transverse directions that encode stability and control are excited only weakly, by intrinsic noise.

<!-- OUTLINE §3 ¶5 --> Gait datasets add further obstacles: tens of strides per trial, a few kinematic channels standing in for a high-dimensional neuromechanical state, discrete contact events, and slow drift in speed and posture. Deviations are a few percent of a trial's variance (Figure [-@fig-gait-mean]B), so measurement noise is not small against the signal a transient analysis uses. On such data the skill any model can reach beyond the mean cycle is small; prediction is tested best where the data hold predictable deviations, after perturbations.

<!-- OUTLINE §3 ¶6 --> Many models fit on-cycle data equally well yet disagree about everything off the cycle, so training loss cannot select among them, and short held-out forecasts do not always either (Figure [-@fig-learnability]A, B; @suppfig-node-gait).

<!-- OUTLINE §3 ¶7 --> When training data contain decays from perturbed states, transverse relaxation becomes identifiable. Even then, recovering it takes many transients and a delay window long enough to span the decay (Figure [-@fig-learnability]C).

![**On-cycle data identify the cycle, not the dynamics around it; transient-rich data make the dynamics learnable, given enough of them.** (A) What 30 cycles of data cover. Left, the slow desynchrony w₁ − w₂ at a Poincaré section; right, the cycle-to-cycle map it implies. The long trajectory barely samples the transverse direction, so even this one-dimensional regression gets the slope wrong (0.27 against a truth of 0.69; decays 0.66). (B) Held-out forecasts do not pin the dynamics: over-parameterised neural ODEs fitted to 10 s of three gait trials (symbols), six seeds each, against the validation error of each fit's autonomous forecast over the held-out 5 s (cumulative RMS relative to the held-out RMS; dotted, the error of forecasting the mean). Left, period of the cycle each learned field settles onto, relative to the stride period (shaded, not a stride-like cycle); right, the transverse multiplier of that cycle (stride-like cycles only). ## Candidate models against the requirements

<!-- OUTLINE §4 ¶1 --> We compare expressive models (neural ODE [@chen2018], echo state network [@jaeger2001], and a spectral-submanifold model [@haller2016; @cenedese2022]) with Hankel-DMD, a linear operator on delay (Hankel) coordinates [@brunton2017; @kutz2016]. Each is tuned on training data only with wide hyperparameter searches and judged by autonomous rollouts on held-out data; the DMD and ESN hyperparameters are themselves chosen by rollout validation on the last two training cycles.

<!-- OUTLINE §4 ¶2 --> **R1, predictive skill.** Where the data hold predictable dynamics, the dynamical models forecast far beyond the reference; on noise-driven data every model's skill is near zero, and what separates them is whether they stay near the reference or fail (Figure [-@fig-selfdriving]C). With 30 clean training cycles, DMD and the ESN forecast the first held-out cycle almost exactly (skill +0.6 to +1.0 against the mean cycle), the neural ODE and SSMLearnPy less well. With 12 noisy cycles, DMD stays within −0.43 to +0.17 of the reference on every system; the ESN forecasts better than DMD on five of nine but falls far below the reference on three; and on held-out gait no model forecasts beyond the mean cycle (@suppfig-forecast). Off the cycle, trained on the same 10 decays, started from real perturbed states, every model tracks the return to the true cycle on SLIP over the first four steps, the single DMD fit most closely; on coupled FHN none does, because each model's cycle sits as far from the true cycle as the realistic perturbation, so its runs stall on the wrong cycle (@fig-convex). On kicked SLIP walks linear models predict the next stride's deviation (R² 0.25–0.53), whereas on human gait none does (Figure S[-@suppfig-lattice]D).

![**Hankel-DMD forecasts consistently and keeps the cycle; expressive models are sometimes the best forecasters but often blow up, collapse or change rhythm (R1, R2).** (A) Free runs from the end of a 12-cycle training window in the realistic regime (1% measurement noise; process noise on the simulated systems) for FitzHugh–Nagumo, coupled FHN, coupled Van der Pol, SLIP walking and one able-bodied gait trial. Grey, held-out data; colour, free runs of every seed (ESN, neural ODE), polynomial degree (SSMLearnPy) or rank (DMD), overlaid; runs that leave the frame are cut. Labels give the outcome counts after 30 cycles. (B) Outcome after 30 free-running cycles, pooled over systems and both regimes. (C) Forecast error over the first held-out cycle per system (realistic and long regimes); black bars, the mean-cycle reference forecast, which defines zero skill; points at 10 diverged. DMD and ESN hyperparameters were chosen on the training data only (fitted on all but the last two training cycles, selected by free-run error on those); the neural ODE uses one fixed recipe; SSMLearnPy the configuration tuned on gait.](figures/Fig2_self_driving){#fig-selfdriving fig-alt="Grid of phase portraits of free runs for four model classes on five systems, a bar chart of outcomes after 30 cycles, and first-cycle errors with a mean-cycle reference level."}

<!-- OUTLINE §4 ¶3 --> **R2, long-run behaviour.** Hankel-DMD sustains the correct cycle in 92% of system–regime cells and never blows up; the expressive models succeed in 42–62% and blow up or settle on the wrong attractor in the rest (Figure [-@fig-selfdriving]A, B). Expressive models fail by blowing up, by settling on a wrong period, or by collapsing to a fixed point; DMD fails by decaying slowly, which is benign and predictable because its eigenvalues are constrained. Short-horizon skill does not guarantee the right attractor: among neural ODEs fitted to one gait trial, the best forecaster over 3 held-out seconds settles onto a cycle 15 times the stride period. Multipliers read out of fitted models vary widely across model classes, seeds and hyperparameters, even among models that forecast similarly (@suppfig-floquet-models).

![**Predicting the return to the true cycle from real perturbed states, and what each model's own cycle has learned (R1, R3).** Models trained on the same 10 decays × 3 cycles, warmed up on the true perturbed trajectory and run freely, from 4 off-cycle starts ordered by the truth's rate (black ticks, truth); each fit's rates from the same starts are joined by a thin line. Rate = (deviation over the fifth cycle / over the first)^1/4^, deviation = distance to the curve through the true cycle's samples, for model and truth alike. Hankel-DMD is one least-squares fit; ESN 4 seeds and neural ODE 3 seeds at fixed tuned settings. |error| = mean over starts of |model − truth|, range over seeds; offset = distance of the model's settled cycle from the true cycle (median), below which its deviation cannot fall. (A) Coupled FHN, per cycle: the truth relaxes at 0.69 from every start; every model's cycle is displaced by as much as the perturbation, so its runs stall. (B) SLIP, centre-of-mass state (y, ẋ, ẏ), per step. (C) SLIP: multipliers of each model's own cycle, rotation against modulus per step. DMD, eigenvalues of its operator in the cycle frame (rotation from the nearest harmonic); square, the one next to the 8th harmonic; ESN, the leading eigenvalue of the monodromy of its own settled cycle (closed-loop Jacobians chained over one period, phase eigenvalue removed), one per seed; star, the exact multiplier (0.769 ∠ 13.6°); diamond, the lattice-constrained fit (@suppfig-lattice).](figures/Fig6_linear_affordances){#fig-convex fig-alt="Relaxation rates per start for DMD, ESN seeds and neural-ODE seeds against the truth on coupled FHN and SLIP, and the multipliers of each model's own SLIP cycle as modulus against rotation."}

<!-- OUTLINE §4 ¶4 --> **R3, one answer.** The DMD fit is a least-squares problem with a unique solution for each hyperparameter setting: no seeds, no local minima, and results that vary smoothly with rank and delay. Expressive models give different answers at equal loss.

<!-- OUTLINE §4 ¶5 --> **R4, measurement noise.** In linear models we know how estimation errors bias the result and can correct it; least squares pulls eigenvalues inward, and instrumental variables remove the bias on the SLIP return map (Figure [-@fig-floquet-maps]B, C) [@dawson2016; @hemati2017; @askham2018]. Expressive models trained by one-step or shooting loss inherit the same errors-in-variables bias, with no closed-form handle on it.

<!-- OUTLINE §4 ¶6 --> **R5, data needs.** Hankel-DMD's relaxation rate converges visibly as decays are added (Figure [-@fig-learnability]C). On real 15-s gait trials no model has enough data.

<!-- OUTLINE §4 ¶7 --> **R6, cost and inspection.** Fits take seconds, which makes cross-validation, bootstrap over trials and subjects, and wide hyperparameter sweeps routine; a single neural-ODE fit takes hours.

<!-- OUTLINE §4 ¶8 --> These failures persist with careful training (Box 1).

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon=false}
## Box 1. Neural-ODE pitfalls

Forward Euler at the sample step spirals outward on oscillations; an output nonlinearity biases the vector field; very short shooting windows; latent encoder–decoder non-identifiability; summed weight decay; selection on minibatch loss.

<!-- TODO Box 1: one sentence per pitfall with its consequence; optional controlled degradation test on Stuart–Landau
(OUTLINE §4 ¶8). -->
:::

<!-- OUTLINE §4 ¶10 --> Linearity is not a free lunch. DMD needs transient-rich data and long enough delay windows; on noise-driven data its forecasts stay near the reference, and the best ESN settings forecast better on five of nine cells. A linear model's cycle amplitude is neutral, so its off-cycle deviation plateaus after a few cycles (@suppfig-offcycle). No passive-data model, linear or not, recovers coupling direction. The claim is about meeting the requirements together, with failures that are known and analysable, not about universal accuracy.

## Linear models on real gait: what they show, and where the data stop

<!-- OUTLINE §5 ¶1 --> Most of gait variance lies in the mean cycle. That part is the cycle's shape, not the dynamics around it, and it says least about how gait is controlled. Whole-trajectory operator measures inherit this: most of the companion paper's transient growth at a ⅓-stride window is reproduced by the mean cycle alone (@fig-gait-mean).

![**Gait recordings are mostly the mean cycle, and whole-trajectory operator measures inherit it.** 299 treadmill trials of 15 s from 42 people (able-bodied, AB; higher- and lower-functioning stroke survivors, HF and LF), six sagittal joint angles. (A) One able-bodied trial (14 strides at 124 cm/s): knee angle of every stride (grey) and the mean cycle (black); below, each stride's deviation from the mean cycle. (B) Share of each trial's variance in the deviations against the number of strides in the trial. (C) Transient growth (TG) of the companion paper's operator [@hess2026nonnormality] (delay DMD, rank 70, ridge 10^−4^, stride-rescaled time; TG = max over one stride of ‖Ãᵏ‖) against the delay window: recorded trials (solid) and each trial's mean cycle repeated with no deviations (dashed); medians. Dotted, the companion paper's window (about ⅓ stride). A periodic signal has nothing to amplify, yet over a window shorter than the stride its harmonics are non-orthogonal and TG > 1; at a full-stride window TG = 1. (D) What the deviations add: per-trial Δlog₁₀ TG, recorded minus mean cycle only; median and interquartile range.](figures/Fig5_gait_variability){#fig-gait-mean fig-alt="One gait trial's strides and deviations, deviation share of variance against strides per trial, transient growth against delay window for recorded trials and mean cycle only, and the increase due to deviations."}

<!-- OUTLINE §5 ¶2 --> Identification success is not evidence of dynamics: the mean cycle identifies people at least as well as an operator signature (@suppfig-identification).

<!-- OUTLINE §5 ¶3 --> A linear operator fitted to delay-embedded kinematics describes how deviations evolve: impulse responses, transient growth, and cross-joint transfer. These are the finite-time response operators argued for above, measured on the deviations, not on the mean shape [@hess2026nonnormality].

<!-- OUTLINE §5 ¶4 --> Stride-level dynamics are not identifiable from 15-s trials. Section deviations barely carry over between strides, the instrumental-variable estimate is unstable, and out of trial no linear model predicts the next stride's deviation better than the mean stride (Figure S[-@suppfig-lattice]D).

<!-- OUTLINE §5 ¶5 --> Structure that theory says a limit cycle has can be imposed on a linear model [@kvalheim2021]. Then even short transients identify the multiplier, but the structure cannot create stride-to-stride signal that passive trials lack (@suppfig-lattice). The exact linear form lives in coordinates we do not measure, and finding the cycle and the phase from data is a problem of its own.

## Discussion and recommendations

<!-- OUTLINE §6 ¶1 --> Judge models by how they predict, the way they will be used: score autonomous rollouts on held-out data as skill against reference forecasts, on the full signal and on the deviations, on and off the cycle, and choose hyperparameters by rollout validation, preferably several rollouts from different starts, rather than by training or one-step loss. Then check long-run behaviour, seed spread, measurement noise and data size.

<!-- OUTLINE §6 ¶2 --> Collect transients: design experiments that excite transverse dynamics (perturbations, speed changes, split-belt). With clinical-length recordings, report identifiability and a null, not a multiplier.

<!-- OUTLINE §6 ¶3 --> Report finite-time response, not only asymptotic multipliers, and compute it under uncertainty.

<!-- OUTLINE §6 ¶4 --> Prefer models whose errors can be analysed. Use expressive models as forecasters or embeddings, not as sources of mechanistic stability claims.

<!-- OUTLINE §6 ¶5 --> Outlook: closed-loop identification with perturbations and controlled inputs, and linking operator structure to neural control [@hess2026nonnormality].

## Data accessibility

The gait recordings analysed here are openly available through the dataset described by @winner2023.

## Code accessibility

All code used for simulations, model fitting and figure generation is available at [github.com/michaelhess17/Gait_Modeling_Perspective_Paper](https://github.com/michaelhess17/Gait_Modeling_Perspective_Paper). Run each script from the repository root with `julia --project=. scripts/<name>.jl`; scripts that write caches are run before the figure scripts that read them.

- @fig-floquet-maps: `Fig3_floquet_maps.jl`, from `fig3_slip_maps.jl` (cache/fig3), `slip_truth.jl`
- @fig-learnability: `Fig1_learnability.jl`, from `fig1_coverage_data.jl`, `gait_overparam.jl`, `dmd_delay_sweep.jl`
- @fig-selfdriving: `Fig2_self_driving.jl`, from `self_driving_benchmark.jl`, `dmd_tuning.jl`, `esn_tuning.jl`, `ssm_self_driving.py` (cache/selfdrive)
- @fig-convex: `Fig6_linear_affordances.jl`, from `offcycle_v2.jl`, `slip_decays.jl`, `slip_rotation.jl`
- @fig-gait-mean: `Fig5_gait_variability.jl`, from `fig5_gait_data.jl` (cache/fig5)
- @suppfig-forecast: `FigS1_forecast_baselines.jl`, from `SSM_baselines.py`, `export_forecast_examples.py`
- @suppfig-node-gait: `FigS2_node_gait.jl`, from `gait_overparam.jl`
- @suppfig-floquet-models: `FigS3_floquet_models.jl`, from `floquet_from_models.jl` (cache/floquet)
- @suppfig-offcycle: `FigS4_offcycle.jl`, from `offcycle_v2.jl`
- @suppfig-identification: `FigS5_identification.jl`, from `fig5_gait_data.jl` (cache/fig5)
- @suppfig-validation: `FigS7_validation.jl`, from `validation_criteria.jl` (cache/selfdrive)
- @suppfig-lattice: `FigS6_lattice.jl`, from `figS6_slip_data.jl`, `floquet_lifted.jl`, `gait_lattice.jl`, `gait_lattice_null.jl`, `gait_lattice_speed.jl`

Results reported in the text without a figure: `iv_gait_stride.jl` (stride maps on gait), `iv_gait_operator.jl` (IV on the companion operator), `fig6_bias_correction.jl` (forward–backward and total-least-squares DMD), `dmd_noise_variants.jl` (DMD under measurement noise), `floquet_tuned.jl` (multipliers read out of models), `coupling_benchmark.jl` (coupling direction). Script descriptions are in `scripts/README.md`.

## Supplementary figures {.appendix}

::: {#suppfig-forecast}
![](figures/FigS1_forecast_baselines){fig-alt="Forecast error against lead time for SSMLearnPy and Hankel-DMD with mean-cycle and last-stride reference levels; per-trial errors; example knee-angle forecasts."}

**Forecast skill on held-out gait.** Every method gets the same information (z-scored joint angles up to sample 1000 of each 15-s trial) and is scored on the same held-out targets by the instantaneous RMSE across the six channels. (A) Median error against lead time for the tuned SSMLearnPy delay map and a rank-70 Hankel-DMD (ridge 10^−4^, stabilised; the companion paper's settings), with two reference forecasts that need no dynamics and define zero skill: repeating a phase-aligned mean training cycle (phase template) and repeating the last stride; interquartile range shaded for the template and the SSM. (B) Per trial at 2.7 s lead: SSMLearnPy error against the mean-cycle reference's. (C–E) Knee angle in one representative trial per group.
:::

::: {#suppfig-node-gait}
![](figures/FigS2_node_gait){fig-alt="Hip-knee diagrams of neural-ODE forecasts for three trials, forecast error against lead time, and learned period and multiplier against training loss."}

**Neural ODEs on real gait: a good fit, an unconstrained dynamics.** A deliberately over-parameterised neural ODE (3 × 128, about 35,000 parameters against 3,000 training values), trained by multiple shooting on 10 s of six z-scored joint angles from one trial per group, six random seeds each. (A–C) Hip–knee angle–angle diagrams (limb 1): grey, training strides; black, the held-out 5 s; colour, each seed's autonomous forecast from the last training sample. (D) Forecast error against lead time for every seed, with the phase-aligned mean-cycle template for reference. (E) Period of the cycle each learned field settles onto, relative to the measured stride period, against the validation error of the autonomous forecast over the held-out 5 s. (F) Transverse Floquet multiplier of that cycle against the same validation error: held-out forecasts do not pin the dynamics.
:::

::: {#suppfig-floquet-models}
![](figures/FigS3_floquet_models){fig-alt="Floquet multipliers read out of neural ODEs, ESNs and DMD against the known truth for several systems and data regimes."}

**Floquet multipliers read out of fitted models, against known truth.** For each system and data regime, the transverse multiplier is read from the model's own limit cycle by chaining one-step Jacobians over one period (neural ODE, ESN), or by a variational probe on data-delay windows (Hankel-DMD, coupled FHN only). Neural ODE, 4 seeds on one data set; ESN, 8 seeds on one data set plus one ESN per data realisation (10); DMD, 8 analysis settings (window ½ or 1 cycle × rank 16, 30, 50, 80; least squares) × 10 data realisations. Points are drawn only for runs that settled on a cycle; runs that collapsed or whose period is more than 10% off the data period are marked.
:::

<!-- TODO Fig S3: rebuild from the tuned and decay results (scripts/README.md). -->

::: {#suppfig-offcycle}
![](figures/FigS4_offcycle){fig-alt="Deviation from each model's own attractor against cycles after an off-cycle start, for DMD, ESN and neural-ODE fits and the truth."}

**Off-cycle relaxation of models trained on decays from perturbed starts.** The true system is started off its cycle; each model, warmed up on 170 samples of that trajectory, then runs freely. Deviation is the distance to the nearest point of the model's own attractor (independent of phase), RMS over each cycle, relative to the first cycle; for the truth, the distance to the true cycle, which decays by the multiplier every cycle. One line per fitted model (DMD, tuned setting; ESN and neural ODE, one line per seed), median over 4 start phases; runs that blew up are not drawn.
:::

::: {#suppfig-identification}
![](figures/FigS5_identification){fig-alt="Identification accuracy of individuals from different gait feature families, with chance level."}

**Identifying individuals: the mean cycle does as well as the operator signature.** The companion paper's split-half protocol: each person's trials are split at random into halves, features are averaged per half and z-scored against the able-bodied half-A distribution, and a person is identified when their other half is the nearest (cosine) match among all 42 people. Mean and 95% range over 200 random splits; dashed, chance (1/42). Deviation features can carry within-stride timing jitter and marker artefacts.
:::

::: {#suppfig-lattice}
![](figures/FigS6_lattice){fig-alt="The lattice-constrained model on one SLIP decay, Koopman spectra of the lattice and Hankel-DMD, SLIP off-cycle metrics for all models, gait forecast skill, forecast error against assumed multiplier, and skill under different selection rules."}

**Imposing the limit cycle's structure on a linear model.** (A) The lattice-constrained model on one SLIP decay: state = fitted cycle a(θ) plus one Floquet mode Re[ψ e^μt^ b(θ)]; the phase advances uniformly, the mode shrinks by the multiplier and turns by its rotation every step, and its shape b(θ) repeats every step. (B) A stable limit cycle's Koopman spectrum is a lattice: read relative to the nearest harmonic, every harmonic sits at (0°, 1) and every Floquet sideband at the star. Hankel-DMD (same 10 three-step decays) fits each eigenvalue on its own; the lattice fit returns one value. (C) SLIP off-cycle metrics, 4 starts: |error| of the 4-step relaxation rate (the metric of @fig-convex, before its scoring was corrected) and distance to the true cycle after 25 steps relative to the initial distance. (D) Human gait and kicked SLIP walks: R² of the deviation from the mean stride 1 stride ahead (filled; 2 strides ahead, open) from half a stride of data; median and interquartile range over trials; multiplier and DMD rank chosen on the person's other trials. (E) Forecast error over strides +1 and +2 against the assumed multiplier modulus: kicked SLIP walks have a minimum near the truth; gait profiles are flat at the mean stride's error. (F) Lattice skill with the multiplier chosen out of trial (solid), on the scored strides (dashed), and on stride-shuffled copies of each trial (dotted): on gait about half of the on-test skill is selection, and the rest does not carry over to other trials.
:::

::: {#suppfig-validation}
![](figures/FigS7_validation){fig-alt="Rank correlations between four validation errors and test forecast error for DMD and ESN settings, and the test forecast skill of the setting each criterion chooses."}

**Validate by rollout, not by one-step error.** Every setting of the benchmark's tuning grids (Hankel-DMD, 60 settings of delay depth × rank × variant; ESN, 36 settings × 3 seeds) in each of the 13 system–regime cells, fitted on the training window minus its last two cycles and scored on those two cycles by in-sample one-step error (a training loss), held-out one-step (teacher-forced) error, one held-out rollout from the end of the fitting data, and the mean of 1-cycle rollouts from 5 starts across the held-out cycles (multistart); then refitted on the full training window and run freely. (A) Rank correlation across settings between each validation error and the test forecast error over the first held-out cycle, one dot per cell; bars, medians. (B) Test forecast skill (1 − error / error of the mean-cycle reference forecast) of the setting each criterion would choose, one dot per cell (open, below −3); best on test, the setting with the lowest test error. Numbers: cells in which the chosen setting keeps the right cycle over 30 cycles.
:::
